title: Positive physiological effects of touching sugi (Cryptomeria japonica) with the sole of the feet
research_question: To clarify the physiological effects produced via tactile application of sugi (Cryptomeria japonica) to the sole of the feet, using the brain and autonomic nervous activities as indicators.

participants.description: Female university students (mean age, 21.9 ± 1.9 years) in Japan. None reported physiological or psychiatric disorders, non-smokers, not menstruating.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but implies volunteers from a university setting.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Unpainted sugi (Japanese cedar, Cryptomeria japonica) wood with two different finishes: uzukuri brushing (embossed hard latewood) and sanding (smooth). A similarly sized buffed marble plate served as a control material. Participants touched the materials with the sole of their feet for 90 seconds with eyes closed.

measures.instrument: Near-infrared time-resolved spectroscopy (TRS-20 system, Hamamatsu Photonics K.K.)
Heart Rate Variability (HRV) - Natural logarithm of High Frequency (In(HF)) power component
Heart Rate Variability (HRV) - Natural logarithm of Low Frequency/High Frequency (In(LF/HF)) ratio

measures.construct: Subjective feelings (comfortable, relaxed, natural, warm-cold, uneven-flat, dry-moist, soft-hard)
measures.instrument: Modified Semantic Differential (SD) method (7 pairs of adjectives from 13 scales)

measures.construct: Mood states (Tension-Anxiety, Depression-Dejection, Anger-Hostility, Fatigue-Inertia, Confusion-Bewilderment, Vigor-Activity, Friendliness, Total Mood Disturbance)
measures.instrument: Profile of Mood States Second Edition (POMS2) short version (35 questions)

mechanisms: Physiological relaxation effects of sugi wood, as indicated by decreased prefrontal cortex activity and modulated autonomic nervous system balance (increased parasympathetic, decreased sympathetic).
Tactile properties of wood (warmth, texture, naturalness, softness) contribute to positive subjective evaluations and mood states.
The 'back to nature' theory suggests that exposure to natural environments or nature-derived stimuli induces a relaxed state due to human evolution in natural settings.
moderators: Material finish (uzukuri vs. sanded) for subjective feelings (naturalness, unevenness) and total mood disturbance.
implementation_implications: Tactile stimulation of sugi wood to the sole of the feet can effectively induce physiological relaxation and improve mood states.
Using sugi wood, especially with an uzukuri finish, as a flooring material in modern society could be effective in relieving stress.
The uzukuri finish is perceived as more natural and uneven, and leads to lower total mood disturbance compared to sanded finish, suggesting its potential for enhanced well-being.

tables.description: Details of the samples (thickness, thermal conductivity, arithmetic average roughness, maximum height roughness)

limitations: Only uncoated sugi wood was used; future studies should investigate various types of coatings.
Only tactile stimulation to the soles of the feet was measured; future studies should clarify effects of more active forms of contact (e.g., stroking with hands).
The study population comprised only young, healthy women in their 20s, limiting generalizability to other demographics (males, different age groups, clinical populations).

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractIn Japanese households, it is customary to walk barefoot on wood floors. This study sought to clarify the physiological effects produced via tactile application of sugi (Cryptomeria japonica) to the sole of the feet, using the brain and autonomic nervous activities as indicators. Twenty-seven female university students (mean age, 21.9 ± 1.9 years) participated in this study. Oxy-hemoglobin (oxy-Hb) concentrations in the prefrontal cortex were determined using near-infrared time-resolved spectroscopy. High frequency (HF), denoted parasympathetic nervous activity, and low frequency (LF)/HF indicated sympathetic nervous activity; both were measured using heart rate variability. The wooden material was unpainted sugi wood with two different finishes uzukuri brushing or sanding. A similarly sized marble plate served as a control. The sole of the feet of each participant touched each material for 90 s. The results found that the uzukuri wood significantly decreased oxy-Hb concentration in the left prefrontal cortex compared with touching the marble. Furthermore, compared to before contact, the uzukuri wood showed significantly decreased oxy-Hb concentrations in the right prefrontal cortex, increased ln(HF), and decreased the ln(LF/HF) ratio. Moreover, the contact with sanded wood significantly decreased oxy-Hb concentrations in the right prefrontal cortex compared with before contact. Thus, it is concluded that tactile application of sugi to the sole of the feet induced physiological relaxation.
